description: Every routine item resolved for the station, with base and effective cadence and which triggers run automatically. Illustrative only: not seed data.

items.name: Daily check: symptoms, sleep and mood
items.plain: Answer three short questions each day: anything new in your body, how you slept, and how your mood is.
items.why: Small changes are easiest to catch early, and astronauts often sleep less than they need. Your own answers, day after day, build the baseline that every other reading is compared with.
items.instrument: The app; the wrist band offers a sleep estimate that you confirm or correct
steps: Open Today and tap Daily check.
Symptoms: tap the body area if something is new or worse. If nothing is new, tap Nothing new.
Sleep: look at the wrist band estimate. Keep it if it is right, or change it. Your correction is saved next to the band's number, which is never erased.
Mood: move the slider to how you feel right now. There is no right answer.
If anything feels urgent, press Someone needs help instead of finishing the check.
The check is done when these three questions are answered. Other readings are optional.

effective_cadence.note: add a headache and vision question at the next check and again 2 hours later

items.cadence_text: Add a headache and vision question at the next check and again 2 hours later

triggers.trigger_text: You report a new or worse symptom

new_cadence.note: a follow-up question each morning until you mark it resolved

triggers.trigger_text: Cabin CO2 is above the one-hour limit of 3 mmHg (sensor_limit)

new_cadence.note: add a headache and vision question at the next check and again 2 hours later

triggers.trigger_text: A solar particle event alert

new_cadence.note: ask about nausea, vomiting, tiredness and skin each day for the next 3 days

triggers.trigger_text: You come back from a spacewalk

new_cadence.note: ask about joint pain, numbness, itching or rash that evening and the next morning

triggers.trigger_text: Sleep under 6 hours (band estimate or your own answer)

new_cadence.note: offer the reaction test that morning

items.name: Blood pressure
items.plain: Rest, then take two or three cuff readings one minute apart on your upper arm.
items.why: Spaceflight shifts body fluids toward the head and changes how blood pressure is controlled. High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so it is only found by measuring.
steps: Empty your bladder. No food, caffeine or exercise in the last 30 minutes.
Rest for at least 5 minutes, 10 is better. In weightlessness, use foot loops or a strap to hold a seated posture with your back against a support.
Bare your upper arm. Keep the arm supported at heart level.
Wrap the cuff snugly. Its lower edge sits about 2.5 cm above the bend of your elbow.
Press start and stay still and quiet while it measures.
Take 2 or 3 readings, 1 minute apart. Save all of them with the time.

triggers.trigger_text: Headache, dizziness, fainting, or a change in vision

new_cadence.note: measure now, then daily for 3 days

triggers.trigger_text: A reading outside your usual range

new_cadence.note: for 5 days, morning and evening readings, then the crew medical officer decides

triggers.trigger_text: Return to gravity (landing on Earth, the Moon or Mars)

new_cadence.note: sitting and standing, with a crewmate ready to help

triggers.trigger_text: Before and after each spacewalk (part of the pre and post spacewalk exam)

items.name: Vision self-check: near reading card and Amsler grid
items.plain: Read the near card and look at the Amsler grid, one eye at a time, and note anything blurred, wavy or missing.
items.why: Long missions can change the shape of the eye and blur near vision (SANS). Most crew on long flights show some signs, and the risk grows with time in space. A quick self-check finds changes between the formal eye exams.
items.instrument: Near reading card and Amsler grid card (paper or on screen at a fixed size)
steps: Wear the glasses you normally use for reading. Use good light.
Hold the card at your usual reading distance; for the Amsler grid, 30 to 38 cm.
Cover one eye.
Near card: read the smallest line you can and save it.
Amsler grid: look straight at the centre dot. Without moving your eye, notice whether any lines look blurry, wavy, dark or missing.
Repeat with the other eye.
Answer the short vision questions: blurred near vision, headaches, eye pain.

base_cadence.note: formal tests at flight day 30, flight day 90 and 30 days before return

effective_cadence.note: while CO2 stays above the limit

items.cadence_text: While CO2 stays above the limit

triggers.trigger_text: Blurred near vision, a new distortion on the grid, or headaches

new_cadence.note: and tell the crew medical officer and the ground

triggers.trigger_text: Cabin CO2 above the one-hour limit (sensor_limit)

new_cadence.note: while CO2 stays above the limit

triggers.trigger_text: Flight day 30, flight day 90 and 30 days before return

new_cadence.event: flight day 30, flight day 90 and 30 days before return
new_cadence.note: formal vision tests with the ground

triggers.trigger_text: Sudden loss of vision, a dark shadow, or severe eye pain

new_cadence.note: urgent: press Someone needs help

items.name: Reaction test (PVT-B, 3 minutes)
items.plain: Tap the screen as fast as you can each time the counter appears, for 3 minutes.
items.why: Tiredness slows your reactions before you notice it yourself. This short test is the same kind NASA used on the ISS and shows when sleep loss is affecting you.
items.instrument: The app reaction test (PVT-B style); a quiet spot
steps: Find a quiet spot where you will not be interrupted for 4 minutes.
Answer the short questions on how tired, stressed and sleepy you feel.
Watch the box. When the counter appears, tap as fast as you can.
Do not tap before it appears. Early taps count as errors.
Keep going until the 3 minutes end. The app compares the result with your own usual speed.
Note any distraction during the test.

base_cadence.note: morning after waking and evening before sleep on test days

triggers.trigger_text: Sleep under 6 hours

new_cadence.note: one test that morning

triggers.trigger_text: A sleep shift or schedule change

new_cadence.note: during the shift and for 3 days after

triggers.trigger_text: Before a spacewalk or other critical task
Head injury or illness

new_cadence.note: with the crew medical officer

triggers.trigger_text: After landing on Earth

new_cadence.note: daily for the first week, then 30, 60 and 90 days after landing

items.name: Exercise session and log
items.plain: Do your prescribed exercise and log what you did, how long, and anything that hurt.
items.why: Without gravity, muscle, bone and heart fitness fall. Daily exercise is the main protection, and you need that strength to walk, egress and work after landing.
items.instrument: Habitat exercise devices; wrist band for activity and pulse; the app log
steps: Do the session your strength and conditioning team prescribed.
Log the device, minutes and how hard it felt.
Note any pain, joint trouble or dizziness. Do not push through sharp pain.
If you missed a session, log the reason. A missed session is never filled in for you.

triggers.trigger_text: Two missed sessions in a row

new_cadence.note: a reminder the next morning and a note to the crew medical officer

triggers.trigger_text: New muscle or joint pain, or a shoulder problem after a spacewalk

new_cadence.note: stop that exercise and tell the crew medical officer

triggers.trigger_text: After landing on Earth

new_cadence.note: reconditioning 2 hours a day, 7 days a week, for 45 days from the day after landing

items.name: Body mass
items.plain: Measure your body mass on the habitat's mass device at the same time of day each week.
items.why: Crews often eat less than they need in flight, and losing mass can mean losing muscle and bone. Tracking it shows early whether you are eating enough.
items.instrument: Mass measurement device (ISS class, for example SLAMMD); not in this kit
steps: Measure at the same time of day each week, before eating and after using the toilet.
Wear the same light clothing each time.
Follow the device's own instructions to the end.
Save the number and the device used.
On the Moon or Mars, a scale made for Earth reads weight, not mass, and reads low. Use the device the habitat provides for mass.

triggers.trigger_text: Mass falls compared with your usual (amount to be set by clinical review)

new_cadence.note: until stable, and tell the crew medical officer

triggers.trigger_text: Poor appetite, nausea or vomiting for more than a day

items.name: Weekly wellbeing self-check
items.plain: Once a week, rate sleep, tiredness, workload, morale, relationships and mood, privately, to bring to your private conferences.
items.why: Isolation, workload and distance from home wear people down slowly. The same topics flight psychologists ask about every two weeks help you notice changes yourself.
items.instrument: The app (private; never shared without your choice)
steps: Find a private moment.
Rate each topic: sleep, tiredness, workload, your morale, the crew's morale, relationships with the crew and the ground, mood, family and personal life, and the habitat (food, noise, space).
Add a note if you want. It stays private.
Choose whether to share any of it at your next private conference.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, press Someone needs help now.

triggers.trigger_text: Mood below your usual on several daily checks (how many to be set by clinical review)

new_cadence.note: and offer an extra private conference

triggers.trigger_text: The death of a crewmember

new_cadence.note: extra private psychological conferences, alone or as a group

triggers.trigger_text: A crew emergency, a serious injury, or bad news from home

new_cadence.note: offer an extra private conference

items.name: Monthly thinking test (WinSCAT class)
items.plain: Once a month, take the longer computer thinking test that ISS crews use, so changes after an injury or illness can be judged.
items.why: A monthly result gives a known baseline. If someone hits their head or becomes ill, the crew can compare and see how much thinking is affected and whether it recovers.
items.instrument: Cognitive test software such as WinSCAT, if the vehicle carries it; not in this kit
steps: Pick a quiet time when you are not rushed.
Start the test and follow its on-screen instructions.
Finish all parts in one sitting.
The result goes to the ground team, who compare it with your pre-flight baseline.

triggers.trigger_text: A head injury, or an illness that affects thinking

new_cadence.note: with the crew medical officer and the ground

items.name: Hearing check (on-orbit hearing assessment)
items.plain: Take the headphone hearing test in a quiet spot so flight surgeons can see any change in your hearing.
items.why: Habitat fans and equipment are noisy all day and night. Hearing can shift without you noticing, and ISS tests have found shifts in many crewmembers.
items.instrument: Audiometer with headphones (ISS class, for example the on-orbit hearing assessment kit); not in this kit. Without it, the hearing questions in the daily check
steps: Go to the quietest place in the habitat. Switch off nearby fans you are allowed to switch off.
Put on the test headphones and follow the instructions.
Press the button each time you hear a tone, even a very faint one.
Test both ears.
The result goes to the ground for review.

base_cadence.note: if an audiometer is carried; otherwise hearing questions only

effective_cadence.note: if an audiometer is carried; otherwise hearing questions only

items.cadence_text: If an audiometer is carried; otherwise hearing questions only

triggers.trigger_text: Ringing in the ears or muffled hearing, especially after a loud event

new_cadence.note: test within a day and tell the crew medical officer

triggers.trigger_text: Noise dosimetry above the flight rule level

new_cadence.note: hearing test at the next opportunity

items.name: Medical emergency drill
items.plain: Practise a medical emergency as a crew: who does what, where the kit is, and how to use the Someone needs help screen.
items.why: Skills fade between training and a real emergency, which may come months later. A drill keeps everyone ready, not only the medical officer.
items.instrument: Emergency medical kit; the app's Someone needs help screen in drill mode
steps: The crew medical officer picks a scenario from the drill list.
One person plays the patient. Another presses Someone needs help in drill mode.
Run the fixed emergency steps. Fetch and open the real kit.
Practise each skill with its teach steps and camera checks: the pulse check on a crewmate's real wrist, chest compressions on a manikin, if listed. The camera's numbers show live and are not stored.
Practise the log for the ground: preview it and press Tell the ground. It leaves at the next contact, and nothing in the drill waits for it.
Debrief: what was slow, what was missing. Log it. Completing the drill updates each participant's skill record and counts toward the practice patches.

triggers.trigger_text: A new module or a visiting vehicle

new_cadence.note: emergency response review

triggers.trigger_text: After a real medical emergency

new_cadence.note: debrief and repeat the drill

items.name: Before a spacewalk
items.plain: In the day before a spacewalk, do a short health check and a private talk with the flight surgeon, who must clear you.
items.why: A spacewalk is hard physical work in a pressurized suit. A cold, short sleep, dehydration or an injury can turn into a real problem outside, so each person is cleared first by the medical officer aboard, as in the onboard procedure.
items.instrument: Kit cuff, oximeter, thermometer, camera station; reaction test; personal dosimeter
steps: Answer the pre-spacewalk questions: new symptoms, ear or sinus problems, sleep, pain, mood.
Take pulse, blood pressure, blood oxygen and temperature.
Drink to stay well hydrated, as prescribed.
Check your hands: trim nails short and note any sore fingertips or nails.
Read and save your dosimeter.

The medical officer clears you before suiting up, as in the onboard procedure. When the link is up, also join the private medical conference within 24 hours before; the flight surgeon's advice goes into that decision. Log it for the ground.

triggers.trigger_text: Any new symptom, short sleep or illness before a planned spacewalk

new_cadence.note: the medical officer checks again before suiting up; log it for the ground

items.name: After a spacewalk: bends, hands, shoulders
items.plain: After the suit comes off, check for signs of the bends, look at your hands and nails, note shoulder pain, and talk privately with the flight surgeon within a day.
items.why: Decompression sickness (the bends) can start hours after a spacewalk, and people tend to play down mild symptoms. Gloves often injure fingertips and nails, and suits strain shoulders.
items.instrument: The app; kit oximeter and cuff; camera of the tablet for hand photos; personal dosimeter
steps: Report at once, never wait: joint or muscle pain, itching, a blotchy rash, numbness, tingling, weakness, dizziness, trouble thinking, or trouble breathing.
If any of these appear, press Someone needs help. Do not do hard exercise.
Look at each finger and nail. Note lifted or dark nails, blisters, sore knuckles or numb fingertips. Take a photo if asked.
Move each shoulder through its full range. Note pain or catching.
Take pulse and blood oxygen. Read and save your dosimeter.
On the Moon or Mars, also do the dust check.
Join the private medical conference within 24 hours.

triggers.trigger_text: Any symptom that could be decompression sickness

new_cadence.note: emergency route at once

triggers.trigger_text: No symptoms at the first check

new_cadence.note: repeat the bends questions that evening and next morning

triggers.trigger_text: Nail, finger or shoulder injury found

new_cadence.note: look and photo each day until healed; crew medical officer decides
